title: Machine Learning Pipelines
abstract:
A pipeline chains every preprocessing step and the model into a single workflow,
so that one .fit() handles everything. This document covers what a
pipeline is, the four properties that make it non-optional in production —
it ensures the same steps run at training, validation and inference; any step can
be swapped or tuned without changing downstream code; it integrates directly with
GridSearchCV and RandomizedSearchCV; and it reduces manual error — plus the
cross-validation leakage it prevents, custom transformers, and how to serialise
and serve one.

blocks.t: What a Pipeline Is
From the notes
Raw data $\to$ preprocess $\to$ model training $\to$ predict.

An ML pipeline is a way to chain all preprocessing steps and the model
into a single workflow. It ensures the same steps are performed during
training, validation and inference (testing the model on real world data).
One .fit() handles everything.
pipeline = Pipeline([ ('step1', transformer1), ('step2', transformer2), ('model', estimator) ])

Every entry except the last must be a transformer (it implements
fit and transform). The last is an estimator (it implements
fit and predict). Calling pipeline.fit(X, y) runs
fit_transform down the chain and fit on the final step; calling
pipeline.predict(X) runs transform down the chain and
predict at the end.
Why It Is Not Optional

blocks.cap:
Without a pipeline there are two code paths — the notebook that
 trained the model and the service that serves it — and they must agree
 exactly. With a pipeline there is one object, serialised once and used in both
 places.

blocks.t: Property 1 — The same steps at training, validation and inference

This is the notes' first point and it is the important one. The overwhelmingly
most common ML production bug is training/serving skew: the
transformation applied at serve time differs from the one applied at training
time.

head: Typical skew bug
What a pipeline does
rows: Production imputes with $0$; training imputed with the median
The median is stored inside the fitted imputer
Production one-hot encodes in a different column order
The category list and order are stored in the encoder
Production forgets to scale at all
There is no step to forget — it is one call
A new category appears and production crashes
handle_unknown is part of the serialised object

blocks.t: The structural argument

Skew is not prevented by discipline or documentation — it is prevented by
making the two paths the same object. If model.pkl contains the
imputer, the encoder, the scaler and the estimator, there is nothing left for
production to reimplement incorrectly.
Property 2 — Any step can be swapped or tuned
From the notes
Any step can be swapped or tuned without changing the downstream code.

Replace StandardScaler() with RobustScaler() and nothing else
changes — not the model, not the evaluation code, not the serving code. The
pipeline is an interface boundary.
Property 3 — Integrates with GridSearchCV / RandomizedSearchCV
From the notes
Pipelines integrate directly with GridSearchCV and RandomizedSearchCV.

Because a pipeline is itself an estimator with get_params, you can search
over preprocessing choices and model hyperparameters simultaneously,
addressed by the double-underscore path step__parameter. This is how you
answer "median or mean imputation?" with evidence instead of habit.
Property 4 — Reduces manual error, allows end-to-end evaluation
The leakage a pipeline prevents inside cross-validation
This is the subtle one, and it is the reason pipelines matter even in a notebook.

blocks.cap:
Left: scaling the whole dataset before calling cross_val_score
 means the scaler's mean and standard deviation were computed using every
 validation fold. Each fold is therefore contaminated and the CV estimate is
 optimistic. Right: with a pipeline, scikit-learn refits the scaler on the
 training folds of each split, leaving the held-out fold untouched.

blocks.t: How large is the effect?

The bias grows as the sample size shrinks and as the transformer learns more from
the data. Scaling leaks two numbers per feature and typically inflates CV
accuracy by a fraction of a point. Feature selection leaks far more —
selecting the top-$k$ features using all the data, then cross-validating, can
produce apparently excellent accuracy on pure noise, because the selection
already used the labels of every validation fold. The same applies to
oversampling: SMOTE before splitting places synthetic copies of a
training row into the validation fold.
Resampling needs imblearn's Pipeline

scikit-learn's Pipeline calls fit_transform on every intermediate
step, which cannot change the number of rows. For SMOTE and other resamplers you
need imblearn.pipeline.Pipeline, which resamples during fit only
and leaves predict untouched — exactly the correct behaviour.
Custom Steps
Any object with fit and transform can go in a pipeline. Two routes:

rows: Wraps a stateless function (log, ratio, clipping). Covered in Topic 18
When the step must learn something in fit — a threshold, a category list, a set of column means

blocks.t: A custom transformer must learn in fit, not in transform

If your transform method computes a statistic from the data it is given,
it will compute a different statistic on the test set — which is
precisely the leak pipelines exist to prevent. Store everything learned as an
attribute in fit (by convention with a trailing underscore, e.g.
self.medians_) and only apply it in transform.
Code

import numpy as np, pandas as pd, joblib
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline, make_pipeline
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, RobustScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_classif
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import (train_test_split, cross_val_score,
                                     GridSearchCV, RandomizedSearchCV)
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 3000
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "age":    rng.integers(18, 70, n).astype(float),
    "income": rng.lognormal(10.5, .6, n),
    "city":   rng.choice(["mumbai", "delhi", "pune"], n),
    "plan":   rng.choice(["basic", "premium"], n),
})
df.loc[rng.random(n) < .1, "income"] = np.nan
y = (df.age + rng.normal(0, 8, n) > 44).astype(int)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(df, y, test_size=.25, random_state=0)

# =====================================================================
# 1. THE BASIC SHAPE -- exactly the syntax from the notes
# =====================================================================
pre = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
                      ("scale",  StandardScaler())]), ["age", "income"]),
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", drop="first"), ["city", "plan"]),
])

pipe = Pipeline([
    ("step1", pre),                                    # transformer
    ("step2", SelectKBest(f_classif, k=4)),            # transformer
    ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),      # estimator (last)
])

pipe.fit(X_tr, y_tr)                    # ONE .fit() handles everything
print("test accuracy:", pipe.score(X_te, y_te))
print("predictions:", pipe.predict(X_te[:5]))
# Raw dataframe in, prediction out. No manual transform anywhere.

# =====================================================================
# 2. PROPERTY 4 -- the leakage a pipeline prevents in cross-validation
# =====================================================================
Xn = df[["age", "income"]].fillna(df.income.median()).values

# WRONG: the scaler sees every fold before CV even starts
X_leaky = StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xn)
leaky = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(), X_leaky, y, cv=5).mean()

# RIGHT: the scaler is refitted on the training folds of each split
clean = cross_val_score(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression()),
                        Xn, y, cv=5).mean()
print(f"leaky CV {leaky:.4f}   clean CV {clean:.4f}")

# The effect is small for scaling but LARGE for feature selection:
Xnoise = rng.normal(0, 1, (200, 5000))          # PURE NOISE
ynoise = rng.integers(0, 2, 200)

sel = SelectKBest(f_classif, k=20).fit(Xnoise, ynoise)   # used ALL labels
print("selection outside CV:",
      cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=500),
                      sel.transform(Xnoise), ynoise, cv=5).mean().round(3))
print("selection inside pipeline:",
      cross_val_score(make_pipeline(SelectKBest(f_classif, k=20),
                                    LogisticRegression(max_iter=500)),
                      Xnoise, ynoise, cv=5).mean().round(3))
# ~0.75 vs ~0.50 on random noise. The first number is entirely an artefact.

# =====================================================================
# 3. PROPERTY 2 & 3 -- swap steps and tune them, in one search
# =====================================================================
grid = GridSearchCV(pipe, {
    "step1__num__impute__strategy": ["median", "mean"],   # preprocessing choice
    "step1__num__scale":            [StandardScaler(), RobustScaler()],  # SWAP
    "step2__k":                     [2, 4, 6],
    "model__C":                     [0.1, 1.0, 10.0],
}, cv=5, n_jobs=-1, scoring="roc_auc").fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print("best:", grid.best_params_)
print("best cv auc:", round(grid.best_score_, 4))
# "median or mean?" is now answered with evidence, not habit.

# Swapping the MODEL itself requires no other change:
pipe.set_params(model=RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=0))
pipe.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print("with a forest instead:", pipe.score(X_te, y_te))

# =====================================================================
# 4. A CUSTOM TRANSFORMER -- learn in fit(), apply in transform()
# =====================================================================
class OutlierCapper(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
    """Cap each column at the IQR fences learned FROM TRAINING DATA."""

    def __init__(self, factor=1.5):
        self.factor = factor

    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
        q1, q3 = np.nanpercentile(X, [25, 75], axis=0)
        iqr = q3 - q1
        self.lower_ = q1 - self.factor * iqr    # trailing underscore = learned
        self.upper_ = q3 + self.factor * iqr
        return self                              # fit ALWAYS returns self

    def transform(self, X):
        # uses the STORED fences -- never recomputes them on new data
        return np.clip(np.asarray(X, dtype=float), self.lower_, self.upper_)

    def get_feature_names_out(self, input_features=None):
        return np.asarray(input_features, dtype=object)

capped = Pipeline([
    ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
    ("cap",    OutlierCapper(factor=1.5)),       # slots straight in
    ("scale",  StandardScaler()),
    ("model",  LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
]).fit(X_tr[["age", "income"]], y_tr)
print("with outlier capping:", capped.score(X_te[["age", "income"]], y_te))
print("fences learned from TRAIN:", capped.named_steps["cap"].upper_.round(1))

# =====================================================================
# 5. RESAMPLING NEEDS imblearn's Pipeline
# =====================================================================
# from imblearn.pipeline import Pipeline as ImbPipeline
# from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTE
# imb = ImbPipeline([("pre", pre), ("smote", SMOTE()), ("model", LogisticRegression())])
# SMOTE runs during fit() only, never during predict() -- which is correct.
# sklearn's own Pipeline cannot do this: transform() may not change row count.

# =====================================================================
# 6. SERIALISE AND SERVE -- the whole point
# =====================================================================
final = grid.best_estimator_
joblib.dump(final, "model_v1.joblib")

# ---- in the serving process, a completely different machine ----
loaded = joblib.load("model_v1.joblib")
incoming = pd.DataFrame([{"age": 34.0, "income": np.nan,      # NaN handled
                          "city": "chennai",                  # UNSEEN category
                          "plan": "premium"}])
print("live prediction:", loaded.predict_proba(incoming)[0].round(3))
# Imputation, encoding, scaling, selection and the model all applied,
# with the parameters learned at training time. Nothing to reimplement.

# The skew test that belongs in your deployment checks:
assert np.allclose(loaded.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1],
                   final.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]), "SKEW DETECTED"
print("skew test passed")

# =====================================================================
# 7. INSPECTING A FITTED PIPELINE
# =====================================================================
print("steps:", list(final.named_steps))
print("learned medians:",
      final.named_steps["step1"].named_transformers_["num"]
           .named_steps["impute"].statistics_.round(1))
print("selected features:",
      final.named_steps["step1"].get_feature_names_out()[
          final.named_steps["step2"].get_support()])
Worked Examples
What a pipeline does on fit and on predict
Pipeline of three steps: impute, scale, classify. Training data $X_{\text{tr}}$, test data $X_{\text{te}}$.
Call pipe.fit(X_tr, y_tr). Each step is fitted in order, and each output feeds the next:

items: SimpleImputer.fit_transform(X_tr): learns the column means, fills NaNs.
StandardScaler.fit_transform(out): learns $\mu$ and $\sigma$ from the imputed training data.

blocks.t: Call pipe.predict(X_te). Only transform runs for the transformers, using the means and standard deviations stored during fit. The classifier then predicts. Test data never updates any statistic.
Worked numbers. Training column $[2,\,4,\,\text{NaN},\,6]$:

items: A test value $x=7$ becomes $(7-4)/1.414 = 2.12$ using the training $\mu$ and $\sigma$. Re-fitting on the test set would give a different $\mu$ and $\sigma$ and silently leak information.

blocks.t: Why this matters for search. GridSearchCV(pipe, ...) refits the entire pipeline inside each fold, so imputation and scaling are re-learned per fold. Preprocessing done outside the pipeline, before the split, leaks.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
A pipeline chains all preprocessing steps and the model into a
 single workflow: raw data $\to$ preprocess $\to$ model training $\to$
 predict.

It ensures the same steps are performed during training,
 validation and inference. This is what eliminates training/serving skew.

One .fit() handles everything, and one .predict()
 applies everything.

Any step can be swapped or tuned without changing downstream
 code.

Pipelines integrate directly with GridSearchCV and
 RandomizedSearchCV via the step__parameter path, so preprocessing
 choices become tunable hyperparameters.

They reduce manual error and allow end-to-end evaluation — and
 critically, they prevent cross-validation leakage by refitting every
 transformer on each split's training folds.

The leak is small for scaling and enormous for feature selection
 and resampling.

Custom steps must learn in fit (stored with a trailing
 underscore) and only apply in transform.
Serialise the whole pipeline, never just the estimator.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Why use a pipeline instead of transforming manually?

Three reasons: it guarantees training and serving apply identical
transformations with identical learned parameters; it prevents leakage inside
cross-validation by refitting per fold; and it makes preprocessing choices
tunable by grid search.

Q. You scaled the data and then called cross_val_score. What is
wrong?

The scaler's mean and standard deviation were computed using every fold,
including the ones held out for validation. Each validation fold is contaminated
and the CV score is optimistic. Put the scaler inside a pipeline so it is refitted
on the training folds of each split.
Q. How much does that leak actually matter?

For scaling, a fraction of a percentage point. For feature selection it is
catastrophic: selecting the top-20 of 5{,}000 pure-noise features using all the
labels, then cross-validating, yields around 75% accuracy on data with no
signal at all.
Q. Why can't you put SMOTE in a scikit-learn pipeline?

Because intermediate steps go through fit_transform, which must preserve
the number of rows, and resampling changes it. Use
imblearn.pipeline.Pipeline, which resamples during fit only and
skips it during predict — you must never resample the data you are
predicting on.
Q. What must a custom transformer implement?

fit(X, y=None) returning self, and transform(X). Inherit
from BaseEstimator and TransformerMixin to get get_params,
set_params and fit_transform for free. Everything learned must be
stored as an attribute in fit and only applied in transform.
Q. What exactly do you deploy?

The entire fitted pipeline object, serialised with joblib, plus pinned library
versions. Deploying only the estimator forces the serving code to reimplement
preprocessing — which is the origin of skew.
